title: Metadata Preservation
prompt_markdown: Which utility helps preserve a wrapped function's metadata?

content.explanation: functools.wraps copies the docstring and name.

title: Stacking Order
prompt_markdown: In what order are stacked decorators applied?
hints: Think about proximity to the function.

content.reference_answer: They are applied from bottom to top, meaning the one closest to the function definition is applied first.

title: functools.wraps purpose
prompt_markdown: Why is `@functools.wraps(fn)` commonly applied to the inner wrapper function of a custom decorator?

choices: It compiles the wrapper function to C for faster execution.
It copies metadata like `__name__` and `__doc__` from the decorated function to the wrapper.
It enables the wrapper to accept asynchronous functions.
It prevents the decorated function from raising exceptions.
content.explanation: Without `@functools.wraps`, the decorated function will report `wrapper` as its `__name__` and lose its original docstring, breaking introspection tools and doc generators.

title: Decorator evaluation order
prompt_markdown: If a function is decorated with `@dec_a` above `@dec_b`, in what order are the decorators applied and executed?
hints: Remember @dec_a @dec_b def f(): ... equals f = dec_a(dec_b(f)).

choices: Applied from bottom to top (`dec_b` first); at runtime `dec_a` runs first.
Applied from top to bottom (`dec_a` first); at runtime `dec_b` runs first.
Decorator order does not affect execution.
content.explanation: Decorators are syntactic sugar: `f = dec_a(dec_b(f))`. Application happens inside-out (bottom-to-top), so `dec_b` wraps `f`, then `dec_a` wraps that. At call time, `dec_a` wrapper executes first.

title: Decorator with Arguments
prompt_markdown: Explain the structure of a decorator that accepts configuration arguments, such as `@retry(times=3)`.
hints: Think about 3 levels of nested functions.

rubric: Mentions three levels of nested functions: factory/outer function, actual decorator, and wrapper function.
Explains that the outer function takes the arguments and returns the decorator.
content.reference_answer: A decorator with arguments requires a 3-layer nested structure: an outer factory function that accepts the configuration parameters (e.g. `times=3`), an intermediate decorator function that takes the target function `fn`, and an innermost `wrapper(*args, **kwargs)` that executes the logic (e.g. loop up to 3 times) and returns the result.

title: Backend Use Cases for Decorators
prompt_markdown: List three widespread production use cases for decorators in backend web frameworks like FastAPI or Flask.

rubric: Identifies at least two distinct cross-cutting concerns (e.g., authentication/permissions, caching/memoization, request timing/metrics, rate limiting).
content.reference_answer: Common backend use cases include: 1) Authentication & Authorization (verifying JWT tokens or user roles before executing the route handler); 2) Performance Caching (checking Redis or in-memory cache before recalculating costly queries); 3) Observability & Metrics (timing request execution and incrementing error metrics).
